findings.title: Queues are unbounded and poll() provides no backpressure
findings.body: Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (line 327) only emits metrics; neither `submit()` nor `poll()` ever blocks. Arroyo's StreamProcessor pulls from Kafka and calls `submit()` as fast as it can, relying on the strategy to push back, so there is nothing limiting how many WorkItems can accumulate in memory. If one group (the exact slow-subscription case this PR is meant to address) backs up, its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps reading, leading to unbounded memory growth / OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is false because the queues never fill and submit never blocks. Use a bounded queue with a blocking put (or make submit/poll block once total in-flight exceeds a limit).

findings.title: submit() swallows exceptions and commits the offset, silently dropping messages
findings.body: The broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` wraps the decoder, the grouping function, and the enqueue. On any exception it calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset`, which marks the offset as processed so the commit thread will commit it, even though the message was never handled. The most realistic trigger is `grouping_fn` (i.e. `ResultsStrategyFactory.build_payload_grouping_key`) raising on a malformed/partial result: that message is then discarded with only a log line and its offset is committed, bypassing any DLQ or retry. This differs from the batched/serial modes where a grouping failure propagates. The message should not be treated as successfully processed (e.g. add to DLQ / let the error propagate) rather than being committed away.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its intent and passes only vacuously
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as 'errors in processing don't block offset commits', but it asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that commits are blocked. That contradicts the implementation: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in a `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises, so both offsets (100 and 101) become committable and WILL be committed. The test only passes because it breaks out after ~0.2s while the commit loop (`_commit_loop`) fires every 1.0s, so `len(committed_offsets) == 0` happens to hold — it is both flaky (slow CI where >1s elapses before the assertion makes it fail) and does not actually test error handling. It should wait deterministically for a commit (like the other tests) and assert the correct behavior.

findings.title: FilteredPayload reaches a decoder that asserts against it; the skip path is only reached via exception
findings.body: `decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, but the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` passes every message's payload (`self.decoder(message.payload)`) to it unconditionally. When a `FilteredPayload` message arrives, the assertion raises `AssertionError`, which is only 'handled' by the new catch-all in `submit` (logging an error per message); the intended `if result is None: complete and return` skip path is never used for filtered messages because `decode_payload` never returns for them. Under `python -O` the assert is stripped and `payload.value` on a FilteredPayload raises `AttributeError` instead (also swallowed). The test `test_handles_invalid_messages` exercises this by sending a FilteredPayload, so it is validating the exception-swallowing fallback rather than the intended skip logic. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly (or `decode_payload` should return None for it) before calling the codec.
